claim: Syllogism difficulty is a stable property of the problem: difficulty ranks agree across six human data sets, and hard problems also give more varied wrong answers.
schema_part: G#/S#: calibrate effort per problem type (S3/S5 depth)
agent_test: Run all 64 syllogism moods at equal tokens; check that the agent's own failure rank correlates with the human rank (Kendall) and that error entropy rises with difficulty.
note: Gap search 2026-10-21: Kendall W .86 / .64 / .45 and entropy-accuracy r = -0.52 re-checked in the author copy of Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012 (N = 156 over six data sets).

claim: No single classic theory (atmosphere, matching, conversion, PSYCOP, PHM, mental models, verbal models) fits human syllogism data; each trades hits against false alarms (mental models 95% hits / 74% correct rejections; conversion 44% / 93%).
schema_part: none
agent_test: Not an agent test. Use as a warning: do not build the scaffold on one theory. Numbers come only from Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012 (re-open failed, see critique).
note: Gap search: hits, correct rejections and correct predictions verified against Table 8 of the author copy of Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012. Still one meta-analysis, so status stays single-source.

claim: Figure (term order) strongly sets which conclusion direction is written; a valid conclusion that fits the bias is drawn by about 80% of people, one that violates it by about 20%.
schema_part: O (re-derive / reorder premises before concluding); G (check conclusion against both directions)
agent_test: Present the same syllogisms in figure 1 and its term-swapped variant; measure accuracy gap with and without an instruction to restate premises in both orders, equal tokens.
note: Gap search: KJL also report correct 'nothing follows' rising by figure (50, 57, 70, 86 percent, Figures 1 to 4). GPT-4o-mini accuracy also falls with figure (F1 89.1, F4 58.7).

claim: Non-reasoning LLMs avoid answering 'nothing follows' (accuracy near 0% on the 37 no-valid-conclusion items under zero-shot CoT in Eisape; at most 32.5% in Bertolazzi; neutral-label accuracy 63.2% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 25.3% for GPT-4o-mini with direct answers). Reasoning-tuned models (o3, GPT-5, Qwen3 thinking, Gemini 2.5/3) reject invalid or existential-import-dependent conclusions at about 99 to 100% in binary tasks and build countermodels at 89 to 99%, so the aversion looks absent there. Nobody has tested free production of 'nothing follows' on the 37 items with a reasoning model.
schema_part: G (explicit 'no conclusion' option), S (a counter-model search state), O (counterexample search)
agent_test: Run the 64-mood production task (nine options incl. 'nothing follows') with a reasoning model and a non-reasoning model at equal tokens; score the 37 invalid items and atmosphere fit.
note: Gap 1: narrowed, not closed. The new data are binary or 3-way tasks with the conclusion supplied, not free production, and have no atmosphere-fit score.

claim: In-context examples do not teach models to say 'nothing follows', even with same-schema examples; supervised fine-tuning does, but fine-tuning is outside our no-training rule.
schema_part: none (rules out few-shot as the fix; points to structure not examples)
agent_test: Replicate with our model: 0, 3, 8 same-schema examples at equal prompt tokens versus a procedural counter-model step. Needs a second study to count as established.

claim: Zero-shot CoT output of LLaMA-3 8B is well predicted by atmosphere (predicts 92.31% of its correct valid conclusions, 82.97% of errors on invalid schemas, 62.79% on valid schemas); LLMs rely on a surface mood heuristic.
schema_part: G (surface-heuristic check), O (verify by independent route)
agent_test: Fit the atmosphere rule to our agent's outputs on the 64 schemas, with and without scaffold; the scaffold should lower the share predicted by atmosphere on invalid items.

claim: Larger and instruction-tuned LLMs beat average human accuracy on syllogisms (best about 75% vs human about 50%) yet keep human-like biases: figural effect, confident errors on the same fallacy items, content/belief effects.
schema_part: G (belief-neutral check, relates to belief-bias document)
agent_test: Run a believable/unbelievable x valid/invalid grid with and without a 'substitute abstract terms' step, equal tokens; measure belief-by-validity interaction.

claim: Scale does not give steady gains on syllogisms: the largest PaLM 2 model was below the second largest, and instruction tuning raised invalid-item accuracy but cut valid-item accuracy (LLaMA-3 70B base 58.89% valid; instruct 54.44% valid, 32.50% invalid).
schema_part: none
agent_test: Track both valid and invalid accuracy for every arm; never report a single pooled number.
note: Gap search: Bertolazzi row mix-up already fixed (70B instruct vs base). No new data.

claim: Offloading deduction to a symbolic solver after LLM translation helps on most logic benchmarks (GPT-4: ProofWriter 52.67 to 79.66, FOLIO 69.11 to 78.92, LogicalDeduction 71.33 to 87.63) but not everywhere: on PrOntoQA Logic-LM 83.20 is below CoT 98.79; LINC did not beat CoT for GPT-4 on FOLIO (McNemar p = .58).
schema_part: O (formal-check operator; use only when translation is reliable)
agent_test: Syllogism to FOL to solver check vs CoT at equal token cost, count translation failures separately from reasoning failures.
note: Gap search: on SemEval-2026 Task 11 (templated, binary validity) ten systems hit 100% / 0 content effect, at least seven of them with a parse-then-prove or checker design. The templated parse is easy; Prontoqa-style exceptions remain.

claim: A solver added only as a tiebreaker on narrow LLM-vote splits works better than a solver as the main judge: tiebreaker 94.3% accuracy, content effect 2.85; Z3 only 74.7%, content effect 26.28.
schema_part: O (verification), G (vote then verify)
agent_test: N=960 SemEval-style set; replicate: 5-sample vote with a solver tiebreak on 3-2 splits versus 5-sample vote alone at equal tokens.
note: Gap 7: partly answered. FregeLogic found Z3-only far worse than vote-plus-tiebreak (74.7 vs 94.3), but UFAL-CUNI (4B model, structured LaTeX parse, Prover9 only) reached 95.8 and ten systems reached 100 with solver-style designs. Difference is parse quality and item template. No paper compares vote-with-tiebreak and parse-then-prove at equal tokens; FregeLogic cost is about 4,300 tokens and 6 calls per item.

claim: Suppression: adding an additional-requirement premise cuts modus ponens (Byrne: 96% to 38%), adding an alternative premise cuts AC and DA (AC 71% to 13%); the effect replicates in direction but is smaller in later work (Dieussaert MP 88/93/60).
schema_part: G (premise-completeness and defeater check), S (assumption listing)
agent_test: Suppression task with LLM: plain vs additional vs alternative premise; measure whether the agent flags defeaters. Note: no LLM study of suppression was found (c27).
note: Gap 3: an LLM version of the suppression design exists (Belief-R, d01 to d03), see K27. Human numbers in this claim are unchanged.

claim: Suppression is graded in the number of counterexamples: disablers lower MP and MT, alternatives lower AC; however, the alternatives effect on DA was NOT significant and disabler presentation raised AC.
schema_part: G (counterexample enumeration depth), S (defeater search)
agent_test: Present 0 to 4 disablers or alternatives to the agent and check graded acceptance; test whether a prompt to enumerate counterexamples first changes the slope.

claim: Content and context matter more than form: with measured sufficiency/necessity, AC and DA rise when a condition is perceived as necessary but not sufficient, and many apparent errors reflect reinterpretation of the premise.
schema_part: G (state the interpretation of 'if' before inferring), S0
agent_test: Compare 'interpret then infer' vs direct inference on suppression-style items; see whether the stated reading predicts the answer.

claim: Judged probability of 'if A then C' tracks the conditional probability P(C|A) for believable conditionals (r = .84 vs .61 for conjunction; mixed-model b = .78 for P(q|p), conjunction b = 0).
schema_part: G (calibration, treat conditionals as probabilistic)
agent_test: Elicit P(if A then C) and P(C|A) from the agent on card-style and everyday items; compute the gap and the share of conjunctive answers.
note: Gap 4: Orth et al. 2026 (d05, d06) test LLMs: all four models respond to P(B|A) (slopes 0.21 to 0.65, vanilla), but conjunction and material readings were not compared.

claim: The Equation P(if A then C)=P(C|A) is weaker when antecedent and consequent are irrelevant to each other (slope .78 positive relevance, .61 negative, .43 irrelevant; N=348 kept of 577).
schema_part: G (relevance check of antecedent to consequent)
agent_test: Give the agent irrelevant-antecedent conditionals ('if the moon is full, then 2+2=4' style); check it does not treat them as simply true or as P(C|A).
note: Gap 4: LLMs respond to relevance but unevenly. Large, few-shot and CoT variants show steeper slopes for negative than positive relations, the opposite of people (.78 positive vs .61 negative).

claim: Humans split into conditional-probability responders and conjunctive responders; the conditional group scores higher on general ability (AH4 98.07 vs 91.65, p=.013, N=115 classified) and endorses fewer AC/DA fallacies, but not more MT.
schema_part: none
agent_test: Classify the agent's responses to the probability task as conditional vs conjunctive reading; check the effect of prompting a 'suppose A' step.
note: Gap 10: no LLM study classifies samples by interpretation style. Orth et al. report ICC .77 to .98 across five samples (d07).

claim: The conditional-probability account of inference (Oaksford, Chater, Larkin 2000) predicts a high-probability-conclusion effect in DA, AC, MT (Exp 1 N=30, F(1,87)=22.90) but its handling of denial inferences (DA, MT) is disputed; the Singmann et al. data fit MP but not MT with probability-logic norms.
schema_part: G (MT is the weak point; check by contrapositive)
agent_test: Vary P(p), P(q), exceptions in descriptions; test whether agent MT acceptance tracks P(not-p|not-q). Pre-register the verdict on MT separately.

claim: Modus tollens is the hardest valid conditional form for people and for LLMs (soft accuracy MP .59, disjunctive .54, MT .31; MT trend lower in high-ability people), and models over-generalize MP/MT/disjunctive syllogism to modal cases where they fail.
schema_part: O (contrapositive restatement), G (modal-scope check)
agent_test: MT items in affirmative and negated forms, with and without 'rewrite as: if not q then not p' step, equal tokens.
note: Gap 5: MT is the weak point in several LLM sets (LogicBench PL(MT) about 59% for GPT-4; Belief-R MT harder; RULEBREAKERS MT below DS). Cause not isolated: negation, backward direction and yes-bias all appear. Contrapositive-rewrite step is untested.

claim: Negation changes conditional inference rates (for 'if not-p then q', MT drops to 35% vs 61% for 'if p then q'), and LLMs that reason step by step collapse when a predicate is replaced by its lexical negation.
schema_part: G (negation-sensitivity check), O (paraphrase and re-derive)
agent_test: Run each item in affirmative, explicit-negation and implicit-negation versions; flag answer changes at equal tokens.

claim: Existential import is a hidden choice: it decides which syllogisms are valid (24 forms under the traditional reading, 15 under the modern one). SemEval-2026 Task 11 states the traditional reading, yet GPT-o3 and GPT-5 sit on the modern reading (accept exactly the 15 modern-valid moods, Acct about 62.5%), and thinking variants of open models drift the same way. Solvers such as Prover9 do not assume existential import and need a patch.
schema_part: G (state assumed semantics: S0 problem restatement)
agent_test: Score our agent on the 9 import-dependent cases under both keys; require it to state the reading used.
note: Gap 8: the benchmark reading is now known (traditional, confirmed by organizers). Stating the reading helps: a prior-check prompt (are the terms empty?) raised modern-logic accuracy by about 3 to 11 points for most Qwen3 models. A prompt that pins the traditional reading was not tested.

claim: Chain length hurts: 3- and 4-premise sets lower zero-shot accuracy, and content effects persist in zero-shot and in-context settings; only fine-tuning removes them (and only with pseudo-words).
schema_part: S (decompose multi-premise to pairwise steps)
agent_test: Chain of 2/3/4 premises solved whole vs stepwise reduction at equal tokens.

claim: Plain CoT does not reliably remove content effects (FregeLogic: CoT raised CE for GPT-OSS-20B from 13.67 to 31.14 and for Maverick from 3.83 to 10.11), but structured prompts do help: rules written into the prompt cut CE from 19.14 to 4.95 for GPT-5, an explicit CoT or strict-logic frame recovered 87% and 76% of GPT-4o failures on belief-inconsistent valid items, and translate-to-logic raised GPT-4 by about 5 points. Activation steering needs model access.
schema_part: none (activation steering outside scaffold scope)
agent_test: Prompt-only abstraction: replace terms with letters, solve, then map back, vs plain CoT, on invalid-plausible items at equal tokens.
note: Gap 9: not a clean abstraction test. No study replaces terms by letters and then lets the same model reason in prose without a checker; the nearest results pair letters with a script checker (Advani) or a prover (0704mis).

claim: Models with similar accuracy can err in opposite ways (one: precision 99.2%, recall 42.8% on validity; another: recall 93.1%, precision 61.0%); a single accuracy number hides over-acceptance versus over-rejection.
schema_part: G (report both error types)
agent_test: Log false accept and false reject separately for each arm.

claim: Reversing the syllogism task (find the missing premise) is much harder than deduction for GPT-4 (abduction about 42% vs deduction 72.22% zero-shot, n=216).
schema_part: O (abduction operator weak spot)
agent_test: Abduction items with and without an enumerate-candidates step.

claim: The mReasoner mental-model simulator fits LLM response patterns, and larger models look more deliberative (System 2) in their errors; mReasoner fits human data at r = 0.82.
schema_part: none
agent_test: Not decision-relevant yet; treat as a diagnostic only.

claim: (Original wording refuted.) It was claimed that no published LLM study tests Byrne-style suppression or the probability of conditionals. Belief-R (Wilie et al. 2024) tests the requirement-versus-alternative third-premise design on 30 LMs, and Orth et al. (2026) test P(if) and relevance. Still untested: reasoning-tuned models on Belief-R, MP/AC/DA/MT acceptance rates with defeater-listing steps, and direct comparison of P(if) against P(C|A), the conjunction and the material conditional.
schema_part: none
agent_test: Run our own suppression and P(if) probes; the result would be new.
note: Gap 3 and gap 4: the earlier search missed these because they use 'belief revision' and 'conditional acceptability' wording.

claim: Belief-R: 30 LMs almost never retract a modus ponens or modus tollens conclusion when a new premise adds a requirement (Belief Update accuracy about 10 to 22% for named API and Llama-3 models, best 44% for Mixtral with plan-and-solve) while keeping it when the new premise is an alternative (maintain accuracy 35 to 92%). CoT and plan-and-solve add about 1 BREU point. Modus tollens bases are harder.
schema_part: G (premise-completeness check), S (defeater search), O (revise conclusion)
agent_test: Run Belief-R with a reasoning-tuned model and with a requirement-vs-alternative classification step at equal tokens; score update and maintain accuracy separately.

claim: RULEBREAKERS: seven LLMs apply modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism rigidly when world knowledge says the formal conclusion should be rejected; GPT-4o and Gemma-2-27b score 100% on ordinary items but worst on rulebreakers (GPT-4o 0.0022 paired accuracy on one modus tollens subset). Models are more confident 'yes' on ordinary than on rulebreaker items, so a latent signal exists.
schema_part: G (check formally valid conclusions against background knowledge)
agent_test: Add a knowledge-conflict probe before accepting a valid-form inference; compare with and without a world-knowledge check step.

claim: LLM conditional probability judgments follow P(B|A) (vanilla slopes 0.21 to 0.65, p < .0001) and respond to relevance, but with weaker and different shape than people: large, few-shot and CoT variants show steeper slopes for negative than positive relations, and Llama 70B vanilla shows almost no relevance effect. Conjunction and material readings were not compared directly.
schema_part: G (relevance check of antecedent to consequent)
agent_test: Elicit P(C|A) and P(if A then C) from the agent on matched relevant, negative and irrelevant items; compare slopes and check the conjunction reading.

claim: Countermodel construction is a separate skill from validity judgment: conventional instruction-tuned LLMs score 0 to 42% on it against about 80% on validity, while Qwen3-32B (89%) and o3 (99%) are near ceiling. Fine-tuning on countermodels alone did not transfer to validity judgment. The model is told the argument is invalid, so noticing invalidity is untested.
schema_part: O (counter-model search) only if the base model is not a reasoning model
agent_test: Test an explicit counter-model step on the 37 invalid syllogisms with a non-reasoning model and a reasoning model at equal tokens.

claim: Content effects on binary validity of supplied conclusions are near zero in several current reasoning-tuned models: belief bias +0.9 to +1.9 points for Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and GLM-4.6; 98.6 to 99.7% accuracy on belief-inconsistent valid syllogisms for GPT-5 variants and Qwen3-32B at medium effort; but 69.2% for GPT-5-nano at minimum effort and +28.0 bias for Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking. The effect depends on the model and effort setting.
schema_part: G (belief-neutral check) is likely unneeded on strong reasoning bases; keep for weaker ones
agent_test: Run the four-quadrant content test (valid/invalid x plausible/implausible) on our base model; skip the debias step if bias is under about 2 points.

claim: Benchmark and model disagree on the logic: SemEval-2026 Task 11 uses the traditional reading with existential import (24 valid moods), while o3 and GPT-5 answer with the modern reading (15 valid moods), and provers like Prover9 do not assume existential import. A system scored on this benchmark must state or patch the reading.
schema_part: S0 (restate existence assumption and the grading logic)
agent_test: Compare accuracy on the 9 existential-import moods with and without an S0 line fixing the traditional reading.

claim: Parse-then-check pipelines reach 100% accuracy and zero content effect on templated SemEval-2026 Task 11 subtask 1 (ten systems), and a 4B reasoning model with a structured LaTeX-to-Prover9 parse reaches 95.8%. Failures are mostly parse errors, label errors and logic-type ambiguity ('It is not true that any'). The templated items make the parse easy, so this may not carry to free text.
schema_part: O (formalize, then verify) with parse-error reporting
agent_test: Report parse error rate and reasoning error rate separately; test on non-templated syllogisms.

claim: In a GPT-5 ablation on 960 SemEval items, writing the Aristotelian rules into the prompt raised accuracy from 78.1% to 89.9% and cut content effect from 19.14 to 4.95; adding a script checker over letter-abstracted terms reached 96.6% and 2.63. Vanilla GPT-5 over-rejected valid items (about 60% on valid, 96% on invalid).
schema_part: S0 / O (rules in prompt before any solver)
agent_test: Add a rules-in-prompt step to the base prompt and measure content effect with and without a solver at equal tokens.

claim: Response style across samples: LLM numeric judgments of conditionals are reproducible (ICC .77 to .98 over five samples at T = 1) but cluster at specific values; no study classifies samples as conditional-probability or conjunctive responders or tests a vote across styles.
schema_part: none yet
agent_test: Sample the agent five times on irrelevant-antecedent conditionals, classify each as P(C|A), conjunction or material, and see whether the vote beats a single run.

claim: Non-reasoning multimodal LLMs rarely say 'neutral' (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 63.2%, GPT-4o-mini 25.3% in natural language, labels only); logic notation, linear diagrams and Euler diagrams do not reliably help; GPT-4 translate-to-predicate-logic then explain gave 83.33% vs 77.78% explanation-only in English (translation 96.67% correct) but hurt GPT-3.5 (52.22% vs 58.89%).
schema_part: O (translate-then-reason) gated on translation accuracy
agent_test: Measure the base model's translation accuracy on 90 syllogisms first; use the translate step only if above about 90%.
